title: Shot Sizes
objective: After this level you can tell a wide shot, a medium shot and a close-up apart and say what each one is good for.
summary: Shot sizes are named by how close the camera is: a wide shot shows the whole body and setting, a medium shot the waist up, a close-up the face and its emotion.

cards.headline: Same actor, same moment, three different feelings.
cards.body: Where you put the camera changes what the audience notices. ACMI explains that filmmakers sort shots by one measure: how close the camera is to its subject, whether that's a character, a setting or an object.

items.label: Wide or long shot
points: The whole body, head to toe
Shows the space around a character

cards.headline: Wide shots tell you where you are
cards.body: Establishing shots show where a scene takes place, and they're usually long shots, ACMI notes. Yale's Film Analysis guide adds that extreme long shots are usually the first or last shots of a sequence. A long shot also shows a whole body moving, which is why it's common in Hollywood musicals and 1970s martial arts films.

cards.headline: Close-ups pull you into a feeling
cards.body: Close-ups are great for showing emotion, and not only big emotions: ACMI points out that one can catch a character trying hard to hide a feeling. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics gives a cinematographer's example: to draw the audience into a key scene, shoot the actors' faces at close range. Sizes are relative, though. Yale notes a close-up is judged against the other shots in the same film.

cards.headline: Shot sizes: framed
learned: Shots are named by the camera's distance from the subject
Wide shot: the whole body and where we are
Medium shot: waist up, for body language
Close-up: a face, and the feeling on it

questions.prompt: Framed from roughly the waist up, a character is in _____.

options.label: a wide shot
options.rationale: A wide shot shows the whole body, head to toe.

options.label: a close-up
options.rationale: In a close-up the head fills the frame.

options.label: an extreme long shot
options.rationale: That shows a whole setting, with people small in it.

questions.explanation: A medium shot, or mid shot, frames a character from about the waist up.

questions.prompt: How does cutting from a wide shot to a close-up change what a viewer takes in?

options.label: It adds more of the setting around the character
options.rationale: That's what a wider shot does.

options.label: It shows the character's whole body in motion
options.rationale: Full-body action needs a long shot.

options.label: It trades the setting for the emotion on a face
It tells the viewer where the scene takes place

questions.explanation: Wide shots show where we are; a close-up fills the frame with a face, drawing you into the character's emotion.

questions.prompt: In The Great Train Robbery (Level 8), the outlaw leader fires his pistol straight at the camera. What shot size was that?

options.label: Extreme long shot
options.rationale: Level 8 describes this shot as a close-up.

options.label: Medium shot
options.rationale: Level 8 describes this shot as a close-up.

options.label: Establishing shot
options.rationale: It didn't show a setting; it showed the outlaw up close.

questions.explanation: Level 8 calls it a close-up: the outlaw fills the frame and fires straight at you.
